title: Quality gate threshold calibration notes (scratchpad) — variance + sensitivity (quant vs caching)
body:
Last updated: 2026-01-09 (SF)

Context / why this doc exists
- Optimize is going to apply batching/caching/quant profile changes that can (sometimes) shift outputs.
- We need pass/fail gates with bounded cost/runtime.
- This is a scratchpad of calibration experiments + variance notes to inform v1 thresholds + how we interpret “small” deltas.

Definitions (working)
- Baseline: current production config for (route, model version, region, GPU SKU) unless otherwise noted.
- Candidate: proposed config diff from Optimize.
- Gate tiers:
  - Smoke gate: fast signal, smaller prompt subset, meant to catch obvious regressions + compatibility issues.
  - Full gate: larger prompt set coverage, statistical confidence for go/no-go.
- Metric types:
  - Binary task success (TS): rubric pass/fail, sometimes auto-graded.
  - Ordinal rubric score (RS): e.g., 1–5.
  - Heuristics: schema validity, function-call JSON validity, refusal/unsafe rate, “empty answer” rate, etc.

Quick summary of what we’re seeing so far
1) Quantization profile changes produce heavier tails in quality deltas than caching/batching.
   - For the same prompt set size, quant changes are more likely to show “rare but bad” failures (long-context, tool output formatting, or hallucination spike).
2) Caching changes generally preserve semantics BUT can create edge regressions via:
   - subtle prompt reconstruction differences (prefix normalization, whitespace, system prompt concatenation)
   - different stop sequence handling under streaming
   - truncation behavior when max context is near limit (KV reuse with different chunk boundaries)
3) Batching policy changes are usually safe semantically; regressions tend to be infrastructure-adjacent:
   - increased tail latency -> timeouts upstream -> perceived quality drop in online signals
   - token streaming cadence changes affecting client-side parsers (not strictly “model quality”)

Experiment setup (calibration runs)
- Harness: eval-harness gating endpoint (pre-prod), paired evals baseline vs candidate.
- We ran paired comparisons where possible (same prompt, same seed policy; caveat: some models nondeterministic).
- Prompt sets used (subset):
  - “optimize.gating.core.v0” (general chat + instruction following)
  - “optimize.gating.tools.v0” (function/tool calling + JSON schema)
  - “optimize.gating.longctx.v0” (8k–32k prompts; long retrieval-ish)
- Models (representative):
  - Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
  - Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct (serving runtime variant)
  - Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (tool-heavy)
- Hardware SKUs sampled: A100-80GB, H100-80GB, L4-24GB (note: baselines differ)
- Candidate change types:
  - Quant: fp16 -> int8, fp16 -> nf4, int8 variant A -> int8 variant B
  - Cache: prefix cache enablement + different cache eviction policy
  - Batch: max_batch_tokens, max_wait_ms adjustments

Variance notes (paired deltas)
Binary task success (TS)
- TS is the most interpretable for “did it work,” but variance is high unless n is reasonably large.
- For paired TS (same prompt judged pass/fail baseline/candidate), I’m using:
  - delta = TS_candidate - TS_baseline
  - Wilson CI per arm (rough), but better: paired McNemar / bootstrap on paired differences.
- Observed noise floor (no-op runs):
  - Across 5 “no-op” runs (identical config, repeated), delta TS mean ~0.00pp, std ~0.25pp on n~400.
  - Tail events: occasionally see -0.8pp to +0.9pp due to judge/model stochasticity on borderline prompts.

Ordinal rubric score (RS)
- RS is more sensitive to “mild degradation” than TS.
- Using paired bootstrap of mean score difference; also tracking fraction of prompts with >=1 point drop.
- No-op runs: mean delta RS ~0.00 to -0.02 (small bias in judge on repeated calls), std ~0.03–0.05 at n~400.

Heuristics (schema validity etc.)
- Much lower variance; these are great smoke-gate candidates.
- Example: JSON validity rate on tool prompts is extremely stable; a 0.5pp drop is already suspicious.

Metric sensitivity by change type
A) Quantization profile changes
What regresses:
- Long-context instruction following: increased “lost the thread” failures.
- Tool output formatting: higher invalid JSON / schema mismatch under some int8 kernels.
- Occasionally higher refusal rate spikes (unclear if causal or just correlated with specific prompts).

Why heavier tails:
- Kernel-level numerical differences can flip a few pivotal logits; the effect is small most of the time, but some prompts are high-gain.

Observed deltas (illustrative; from small calibration set, not final numbers)
- fp16 -> int8 (A100) on general core set (n~600):
  - TS delta median ~ -0.1pp; p10 ~ -0.7pp; p90 ~ +0.4pp
  - RS delta median ~ -0.03; p10 ~ -0.10
- fp16 -> nf4 (L4) on longctx set (n~250):
  - TS delta median ~ -0.4pp; worst run observed ~ -2.0pp (small n; heavy tail)
  - JSON validity: generally unchanged, but one kernel combo showed -1.5pp (this is a red flag)

Takeaway for gating
- Quant changes need:
  - stricter thresholds on tool validity and longctx subsets
  - bigger n (or mandatory reruns) to reduce false negatives
  - baseline selection pinned to (model family, model version, GPU SKU) (see Arjun/Grace notes)

B) Caching (prefix/KV) changes
What regresses:
- Rare prompt reconstruction/normalization issues (whitespace, system prompt boundaries).
- Rare truncation behavior when near context limit.
- “Leaky” cache keying mistakes would be catastrophic, but that should be caught by static validation + invariants tests before gating.

Observed deltas
- Cache enablement for routes with no prior cache (n~800 core, n~300 tools):
  - TS delta generally within +/-0.3pp
  - RS delta within +/-0.04
  - Heuristics: stop token adherence occasionally changes (affects exact-match style checks; need to be careful what we measure)

Takeaway for gating
- For caching, smoke gate should emphasize invariants:
  - no change in tool JSON validity rate
  - no increase in “empty output”
  - no increase in truncation markers / incomplete tool calls
- Full gate can allow slightly larger tolerance than quant, since true regressions seem rarer + smaller.

C) Batching policy changes
What regresses:
- Mostly not semantics; issues show up as:
  - timeouts (online) or “partial generations” if client cancels
  - in harness: can change streaming chunk boundaries (some brittle tests fail)

Observed deltas
- When we keep max tokens and sampling the same, offline TS/RS deltas are basically noise.
- However, batching changes can increase latency variance; quality gate should not try to “grade” that with TS/RS.

Takeaway for gating
- For batching, quality gate should be mostly:
  - correctness invariants + no increase in error rate
  - *plus* separate rollout SLO guardrails (SRE-owned) for latency/timeout

Threshold calibration (v1 proposal — not final)
NOTE: These numbers are what I think will be stable given observed variance. Needs sign-off with Karthik/Jonas/Selene + PM.

Decision structure
- Each gate run returns: pass / fail / inconclusive.
- Inconclusive triggers automatic rerun up to R times (current thought: R=2 for smoke, R=1 for full) and aggregates with flake scoring.

Smoke gates (fast)
Goal: catch obvious regressions + formatting/tool failures quickly.
- n target: 150–250 prompts total across 2–3 suites (core small + tools small + (if quant) longctx small)
- Pass criteria (candidate vs baseline):
  - Tool JSON validity: no drop > 0.5pp AND absolute validity >= 99.0% (whichever is stricter)
  - Empty/aborted output rate: no increase > 0.3pp
  - Task success (core): allow small drop up to 0.7pp if CI overlaps (i.e., don’t fail purely on tiny TS drift at small n)
- Quant-specific smoke add-on:
  - Longctx TS: no drop > 1.0pp at small n; if borderline => rerun

Full gates (slower)
Goal: provide strong confidence before apply / canary promote.
- n target: 1,500–3,000 prompts (depends on route tier); minimum per suite coverage to avoid overfitting core-only.
- Proposed non-inferiority style margins (candidate must not be worse than baseline beyond margin M):
  - Caching / batching:
    - TS: M = 0.5pp
    - RS mean: M = 0.05
    - Tool validity: M = 0.2pp (very strict; we don’t want tool formatting regressions)
  - Quantization:
    - TS: M = 0.3pp (stricter)
    - RS mean: M = 0.04
    - Tool validity: M = 0.2pp
    - Longctx TS: M = 0.4pp (separate check; needs more longctx prompts)

How we decide “pass” statistically (working)
- For TS (binary):
  - Use paired test when we can (McNemar) and require p(non-inferior) >= 0.95 (or equivalently one-sided alpha 0.05)
  - If not paired (due to nondeterminism / judge), use bootstrap over prompts with enough n
- For RS (ordinal):
  - Paired bootstrap of mean delta; require P(delta <= -M) < 0.05
- For heuristics (validity):
  - Treat as binary with strict margin + absolute floor

Rerun policy notes (flake handling)
- We’ve seen flakiness mostly from:
  - judge borderline prompts
  - transient harness timeouts causing missing outputs (should be excluded carefully)
  - model nondeterminism if seed control not enforced
- Proposed rule of thumb:
  - If gate fails only on TS by <0.4pp AND tool validity/heuristics are clean, mark as “inconclusive” and rerun before hard fail.
  - If tool validity fails, hard fail immediately (no rerun unless there’s clear infrastructure incident).
- This lines up with eval-harness flake score work (Olivia) and quarantine workflow (ENG-3929).

Baseline selection gotchas (quant)
- Baseline must be per (model family, model version, GPU SKU, runtime build) because:
  - int8 kernels differ materially across SKUs
  - we saw a case where candidate looked “fine” vs global baseline but was worse vs the correct SKU baseline
- Action item: ensure the gating input contract includes explicit baseline_id that encodes SKU. (Arjun/Grace + Olivia)

Concrete examples / ‘what actually failed’ notes
1) Tool JSON validity regression (quant)
- Qwen2.5-7B tools suite: fp16 -> int8 (L4) had invalid JSON increase from ~0.6% to ~2.0% on a small run.
- That’s a hard fail. Even if TS/RS look okay, this breaks downstream parsers.
- Suspected: kernel path + sampling temp; needs runtime investigation.

2) Caching edge with longctx
- Longctx prompts near max context: cache enablement changed truncation boundary.
- Not a “model quality” change, but user-visible (missing last tool arg).
- We need a heuristic: detect truncated tool call / incomplete JSON more explicitly.

3) Batching change triggering perceived quality drop online
- Offline TS stable, but p95 latency increased, causing timeouts in an upstream customer integration.
- Reminder: quality gate should not be the only guardrail. We need rollout coupling to SLO checks.

Open questions
- What is the right “absolute floor” on TS for certain suites? (e.g., if baseline TS is already low on a route, margins may be meaningless.)
- Should we have route-tier-specific margins? Enterprise routes may demand stricter margins; self-serve might accept slightly larger drift with explicit messaging.
- How do we treat “improvements” that come with variance? (We should pass; but avoid overreacting.)
- Judge model drift: if rubric judge changes, it will move baselines. Need version pinning + backfill.

TODO / next actions
- [SF] Run additional no-op variance study with fixed seeds + judge pinned; quantify remaining noise floor by suite. Target: 10 runs per suite.
- [Karthik + Selene] Confirm which metric is the primary ‘ship stopper’ per config type (TS vs RS vs tool validity).
- [Olivia] Confirm harness returns paired artifacts (per-prompt outcomes) so we can use McNemar/paired bootstrap reliably.
- [Grace + Arjun] Validate quant baselines per SKU and identify “unsafe” kernel combos that should be statically blocked pre-gate.
- [Jonas] Ensure prompt set coverage includes longctx + tools for quant gates; smoke gates must include at least a minimal longctx slice.

Notes to self (messy)
- Our margins can’t be smaller than the measurement noise floor unless we force bigger n or more reruns.
- If we pick M too strict for quant (e.g., 0.1pp TS), we’ll block too many changes and drive overrides.
- If we pick M too loose, we will ship silent regressions and lose trust. Tool validity should be extremely strict; TS/RS can have small tolerances with confidence checks.
